name: BMW M3 (E36)
engine: 3.2L S52 (S52B32) inline-six — US 1996–1999; 1995 US cars used the 3.0L S50B30US, also 240 hp
transmission: 5-speed manual, or a 5-speed automatic (Europe got a 6-speed manual)
reliability: 7/10 — mechanically the E36 M3 is dependable by M-car standards, but two truths define ownership. First, the US car got the detuned S52 (a hot-rodded M50-family six, 240 hp) rather than Europe's exotic individual-throttle-body S50B32 with 316+ hp, so purists argue it isn't a 'real' M3 — it's still a rewarding, affordable driver. Second, the cooling system is a maintenance clock: the plastic thermostat housing, water-pump impeller, radiator, and expansion tank all age out and can cook the engine if ignored. Stay ahead of cooling and VANOS and it's a cheap way into M ownership.
cost_to_own: Insurance: Moderate · Maintenance ~$1,000/yr (cooling and VANOS are the big-ticket items) · Still one of the most affordable ways into an M3, though clean unmodified cars are starting to appreciate
popular_mods: A full cooling-system overhaul (all-metal thermostat housing, water pump, radiator, expansion tank) — do this first
A VANOS rebuild/upgrade to restore crisp midrange and kill the rattle
Coilovers and fresh bushings — the E36 chassis responds beautifully to a suspension refresh
A rear subframe reinforcement on hard-driven or tracked cars
Honest take: sort the cooling and VANOS before chasing power — reliability is the real upgrade on an E36

generations.E36 M3 (1995–1999 US): The M3 grown into a refined, usable coupe/sedan/convertible GT with a smooth inline-six. US cars ran the 240 hp S52 (S50B30US in 1995), trading the Euro car's exotica for value and everyday friendliness.
generations.Euro S50B32 (not sold in US): Europe's 3.2L S50B32 with individual throttle bodies, higher compression, and 316–321 hp is the enthusiast's E36 M3 — a genuinely different, more special engine than the US S52.

common_issues: VANOS rattle and wear — the 'marbles in a can' noise with a midrange power loss
Cooling-system failures — plastic thermostat housing, water-pump impeller, radiator, and expansion tank all age out
Rear subframe / trunk-floor mounting-point cracking on hard-used cars
Oil leaks from the valve-cover and oil-filter-housing gaskets
Cam-position sensor and cooling-fan clutch failures with age
maintenance_tips: Replace the entire cooling system proactively — treat plastic coolant parts as scheduled wear items
Address VANOS with a rebuild kit at the first sign of rattle or lost midrange
Inspect the rear subframe mounts, especially on any car with track history
Use the correct 10W-60 M-spec synthetic and let the six warm before hard use
Keep the gaskets fresh — small oil leaks are cheap to fix and easy to ignore until they aren't

engine.detail: The US S52B32 — a 3.2L version of BMW's iron-block M50-family inline-six making 240 hp and 236 lb-ft at 3,800 rpm, with single VANOS variable intake timing (1995 US cars used the 3.0L S50B30US, also 240 hp). Torquey and durable, if not the exotic 316+ hp individual-throttle-body Euro S50B32.
engine.watch: Cooling is the maintenance clock — the plastic thermostat housing, water-pump impeller, radiator, and expansion tank all age out and can cook the engine if ignored. Expect VANOS rattle ('marbles in a can') with a midrange power loss, plus valve-cover and oil-filter-housing gasket leaks and the odd cam-position sensor or fan clutch.

drivetrain.detail: A 5-speed manual (the one to have) or a 5-speed automatic, driving the rear wheels; Europe got a 6-speed manual.
drivetrain.watch: Dependable by M standards — the manual and rear end are robust; the slushbox auto is the enthusiast's car to avoid.

suspension.detail: MacPherson-strut front and BMW's multilink 'Z-axle' rear — a balanced, communicative chassis that responds beautifully to a refresh.
suspension.watch: Tired bushings and dampers dull it on high-mile cars; fresh bushings and coilovers are the classic first move.

brakes.detail: Vented front and rear discs — plenty of stopping power for a ~3,175 lb coupe.
brakes.watch: Stock brakes are fine on the street; pads, fluid, and cooling ducts are all a track day needs.

body.detail: Steel unibody coupe, sedan, or convertible — the M3 grown into a refined, usable GT.
body.watch: The known weak point is cracking at the rear subframe mounting points and trunk floor on hard-driven or tracked cars — inspect and reinforce. Watch for rust in the usual rockers and arches on neglected examples.
